title: Closed cube in a uniform field
stem: A closed cube with 0.20 m edges contains no charge. It sits in a uniform external electric field of 300 N/C directed perpendicular to two of its faces. What is the net electric flux through the entire surface of the cube?

correct.rationale: Gauss's law gives Φ = Q_enc/ε₀ = 0 because the cube encloses no charge. Directly: the field enters one face with flux −EA = −12 N·m²/C, leaves the opposite face with +12 N·m²/C, and gives zero flux through the four faces parallel to the field.

wrong.rationale: This is the flux magnitude through one face, EA = (300)(0.040) = 12 N·m²/C. The entering face contributes −12 and the leaving face contributes +12, so the net flux is 0.
wrong.error_pattern: reports flux through one face instead of the net flux through the closed surface

wrong.rationale: This adds the magnitudes of the entering and leaving fluxes. Flux is signed: the entering flux is negative and the leaving flux is positive, so they cancel to 0.
wrong.error_pattern: adds magnitudes of inward and outward flux instead of signed sum

wrong.rationale: This treats every one of the six faces as having flux EA. The four faces parallel to the field have zero flux, and the other two cancel, so the net flux is 0.
wrong.error_pattern: applies E·A to all six faces regardless of orientation

change_note: New context: external uniform field and a charge-free cube; seed asked the zero-flux result for an empty closed surface in the abstract; distractors are one face, magnitude sum, six faces.

title: Dipole inside, charge outside
stem: A closed surface encloses a +4.0 nC charge and a −4.0 nC charge. A separate +6.0 nC charge sits outside the surface. What is the net electric flux through the surface?

correct.rationale: Only enclosed charge matters in Gauss's law: Q_enc = +4.0 nC − 4.0 nC = 0, so Φ = 0. The outside charge produces field lines that enter and leave the surface with no net flux.

wrong.rationale: This is (6.0 nC)/ε₀, which counts the outside charge. Charge outside a closed surface contributes zero net flux, and the enclosed charges sum to zero, so the flux is 0.
wrong.error_pattern: includes charge outside the surface in Q_enc

wrong.rationale: This is (4.0 nC)/ε₀, which counts only the enclosed positive charge. The enclosed −4.0 nC cancels it, so Q_enc = 0 and the flux is 0.
wrong.error_pattern: counts only the positive enclosed charge

wrong.rationale: This is (8.0 nC)/ε₀, which adds the magnitudes of the two enclosed charges. Charge is signed, so Q_enc = 0 and the flux is 0.
wrong.error_pattern: adds magnitudes of enclosed charges and ignores sign

change_note: Mixed-sign enclosed charges summing to zero with an outside charge; numbers all new; distractors include outside charge, positive-only and magnitude sum.

title: Gaussian sphere inside a charged shell
stem: A thin, uniformly charged spherical shell of radius 0.20 m carries a total charge of +12 nC. A concentric spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.10 m lies entirely inside the shell. What is the net electric flux through the Gaussian surface?

correct.rationale: The Gaussian sphere lies inside the shell and encloses no charge, because all of the charge sits on the shell's surface. Gauss's law gives Φ = Q_enc/ε₀ = 0.

wrong.rationale: This is (12 nC)/ε₀, the flux through a surface that encloses the whole shell. The smaller sphere is inside the shell and encloses none of its charge.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the total charge of the shell as Q_enc

wrong.rationale: This scales the total charge by the volume ratio (0.10/0.20)³ = 1/8, as if the charge were spread through the volume. The charge is on the shell's surface, so Q_enc = 0.
wrong.error_pattern: treats surface charge as volume-distributed and scales Q_enc by volume fraction

wrong.rationale: This scales the total charge by the area ratio (0.10/0.20)² = 1/4, as if part of the shell's charge were inside the smaller sphere. None of the charge lies inside it, so Q_enc = 0.
wrong.error_pattern: scales Q_enc by area fraction of the shell

change_note: Spherical-symmetry shell with the Gaussian surface in the cavity; same enclosed-charge-zero concept; distractors are total charge, volume fraction, area fraction.

title: Block on a 30° frictionless incline
stem: A 4.0 kg block slides down a frictionless incline that makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the incline on the block?

correct.rationale: The normal force balances the component of weight perpendicular to the surface: N = mg cosθ = (4.0)(10)(cos 30°) ≈ 35 N.

wrong.rationale: This is the full weight mg. The incline's normal force balances only the component of the weight perpendicular to the surface, mg cosθ ≈ 35 N.
wrong.error_pattern: sets normal force equal to the weight

wrong.rationale: This is mg sinθ, the component of weight along the incline, which accelerates the block. The normal force balances the perpendicular component mg cosθ ≈ 35 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the parallel component mg sinθ for the normal force

wrong.rationale: This divides by cosθ: mg/cosθ. The perpendicular component of the weight is mg cosθ, which is smaller than mg, so N ≈ 35 N.
wrong.error_pattern: divides by cosθ instead of multiplying

change_note: New numeric context with a 30° incline; seed was symbolic; distractors are mg, mg sinθ and mg/cosθ.

title: Ramp given by its dimensions
stem: A 2.5 kg crate slides down a frictionless ramp whose horizontal length is 4.0 m and whose height is 3.0 m. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the ramp on the crate?

correct.rationale: The ramp's surface length is 5.0 m, so cosθ = 4.0/5.0 = 0.80. The normal force balances the weight component perpendicular to the surface: N = mg cosθ = (2.5)(10)(0.80) = 20 N.

wrong.rationale: This is mg sinθ = (25)(0.60), the component of weight along the ramp. The normal force uses the perpendicular component, mg cosθ = 20 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the parallel component mg sinθ for the normal force

wrong.rationale: This is the full weight mg. Only the component perpendicular to the ramp is balanced by the normal force, which is mg cosθ = 20 N.
wrong.error_pattern: sets normal force equal to the weight

wrong.rationale: This uses mg tanθ = (25)(3/4), which mixes the height and horizontal length directly. The normal force is mg cosθ, and cosθ = 4.0/5.0 for a 3-4-5 ramp, so N = 20 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses tanθ (rise over run) in place of cosθ

change_note: Angle is given implicitly by the ramp's dimensions, so the student must find cosθ from a 3-4-5 triangle; new numbers; same normal-force concept.

title: Incline angle measured from the vertical
stem: A 2.0 kg block slides down a frictionless plane. The surface of the plane makes an angle of 25° with the vertical. Use g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the normal force exerted by the plane on the block?

correct.rationale: The angle between the surface and the horizontal is 90° − 25° = 65°. The normal force is N = mg cosθ = (20)(cos 65°) ≈ 8.5 N.

wrong.rationale: This uses cos 25°, the angle from the vertical, as if it were the incline angle. The incline angle with the horizontal is 65°, so N = mg cos 65° ≈ 8.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the angle from the vertical as the incline angle

wrong.rationale: This is the full weight mg. The normal force balances only the component of weight perpendicular to the surface, mg cos 65° ≈ 8.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: sets normal force equal to the weight

wrong.rationale: This divides the weight by cos 65°. The perpendicular component of the weight is mg cos 65°, which is smaller than mg, so N ≈ 8.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: divides by cosθ instead of multiplying

change_note: Incline angle is given relative to the vertical, so the student must identify the angle between the surface and the horizontal first; same normal-force concept.

title: Net force from a linear velocity
stem: A 3.0 kg cart of constant mass moves along a straight track with velocity v(t) = (4.0 m/s²)t + 1.0 m/s, where t is in seconds. What is the magnitude of the net force on the cart at t = 2.0 s?

correct.rationale: For constant mass, F_net = m dv/dt. Here dv/dt = 4.0 m/s², so F_net = (3.0)(4.0) = 12 N.

wrong.rationale: This is m v/t = (3.0)(9.0)/(2.0), which divides the velocity by the elapsed time. Net force is mass times the derivative dv/dt = 4.0 m/s², giving 12 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses mv/t instead of m dv/dt

wrong.rationale: This multiplies mass by the velocity at t = 2.0 s, (3.0)(9.0). Net force is mass times the rate of change of velocity, which is 12 N.
wrong.error_pattern: multiplies mass by velocity instead of by dv/dt

wrong.rationale: This is the numerical value of dv/dt with the mass left out. Net force is m dv/dt = (3.0)(4.0) = 12 N.
wrong.error_pattern: omits the mass

change_note: New numeric context with linear v(t); seed asked for the expression; distractors are mv/t, mv and the missing mass.

title: Net force from a cubic velocity
stem: A 1.5 kg block of constant mass moves along a line with velocity v(t) = (2.0 m/s⁴)t³ − (3.0 m/s²)t, where t is in seconds. What is the magnitude of the net force on the block at t = 2.0 s?

correct.rationale: For constant mass, F_net = m dv/dt. dv/dt = 6.0t² − 3.0 = 21 m/s² at t = 2.0 s, so F_net = (1.5)(21) = 31.5 N.

wrong.rationale: This is m v/t = (1.5)(10)/(2.0), which uses the average rate v/t from the start. Net force requires the instantaneous derivative dv/dt = 21 m/s², giving 31.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses mv/t instead of m dv/dt

wrong.rationale: This multiplies mass by the velocity at t = 2.0 s, (1.5)(10). Net force is mass times the derivative of velocity, which gives 31.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: multiplies mass by velocity instead of by dv/dt

wrong.rationale: This integrates the velocity from 0 to 2.0 s, giving a displacement of 2.0 m, and multiplies by the mass. Net force comes from differentiating, not integrating: m dv/dt = 31.5 N.
wrong.error_pattern: integrates v(t) instead of differentiating it

change_note: Cubic v(t) needing a derivative evaluated at an instant; new numbers; distractors are mv/t, mv and integration instead of differentiation.

title: Net force from a position function
stem: A 2.0 kg object of constant mass moves along the x-axis with position x(t) = (0.50 m/s⁴)t⁴ − (2.0 m/s)t, where t is in seconds. What is the magnitude of the net force on the object at t = 1.5 s?

correct.rationale: Velocity is v = dx/dt = 2.0t³ − 2.0. Acceleration is a = dv/dt = 6.0t² = 13.5 m/s² at t = 1.5 s. For constant mass, F_net = m dv/dt = (2.0)(13.5) = 27 N.

wrong.rationale: This is the acceleration at t = 1.5 s with the mass left out. Net force is m dv/dt = (2.0)(13.5) = 27 N.
wrong.error_pattern: omits the mass

wrong.rationale: This is m v at t = 1.5 s, (2.0)(4.75), which takes one derivative of position and treats velocity as acceleration. Net force needs the second derivative of position: 27 N.
wrong.error_pattern: differentiates position only once and multiplies mass by velocity

wrong.rationale: This is the mass times the average acceleration from t = 0 to 1.5 s, (2.0)(6.75/1.5). The acceleration is not constant, so the instantaneous value dv/dt = 13.5 m/s² is needed, giving 27 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses average acceleration over an interval instead of the instantaneous derivative

change_note: Net force from a position function requires two derivatives; new numbers; distractors are missing mass, one derivative and average acceleration.

title: Heating a rigid sealed container
stem: A rigid sealed container holds an ideal gas at 27°C and a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. The gas is heated to 177°C. What is its final pressure?

correct.rationale: At fixed volume and amount, PV = nRT gives P proportional to the absolute temperature. The temperatures are 300 K and 450 K, so P = (1.0 × 10⁵)(450/300) = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa.

wrong.rationale: This uses the ratio of Celsius temperatures, 177/27. Pressure is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so the ratio is 450/300 and P = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa.
wrong.error_pattern: uses Celsius temperatures instead of kelvins

wrong.rationale: This inverts the ratio, 300/450. At fixed volume, pressure increases with temperature, so P = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa.
wrong.error_pattern: inverts the temperature ratio (P inversely proportional to T)

wrong.rationale: This assumes the pressure stays the same because the volume is fixed. With volume and amount fixed, P is proportional to T, so heating raises the pressure to 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa.
wrong.error_pattern: thinks fixed volume means pressure is unchanged

change_note: New context with a Celsius-to-kelvin conversion for the same fixed-volume P proportional to T; seed was a pure doubling ratio; distractors are Celsius ratio, inverted ratio and unchanged pressure.

title: Extrapolating a pressure-temperature line
stem: A rigid vessel holds a fixed amount of ideal gas. Its pressure is 120 kPa at 27°C and 160 kPa at 127°C, and the graph of pressure versus Celsius temperature is a straight line. The line is extended down to zero pressure. At what Celsius temperature does it reach zero pressure?

correct.rationale: At fixed volume P is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so P = 0 at 0 K, which is −273°C. The data agree: 120 kPa at 300 K and 160 kPa at 400 K give 0.40 kPa per kelvin, and 120/0.40 = 300 K below 27°C is −273°C.

wrong.rationale: This assumes the pressure vanishes at the freezing point of water. Pressure is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so it reaches zero at 0 K, which is −273°C.
wrong.error_pattern: places zero pressure at 0°C instead of 0 K

wrong.rationale: This divides 120 kPa by the slope of 0.40 kPa/°C and measures the result from 0°C. The 300°C drop must be measured from the 27°C starting point, giving −273°C.
wrong.error_pattern: measures the extrapolation from 0°C instead of from the 27°C data point

wrong.rationale: This extends the line by one more 100°C measurement interval below 27°C. The line continues until the pressure is zero, which takes a 300°C drop from 27°C, reaching −273°C.
wrong.error_pattern: extrapolates only one measurement interval

change_note: Graph-extrapolation form of the same fixed-volume P proportional to T relationship; new data; distractors are 0°C, offset error and one-interval extrapolation.

title: Tripling the pressure of a sealed gas
stem: A rigid sealed tank holds an ideal gas at 27°C. To what Celsius temperature must the gas be heated so that its pressure becomes three times its initial value?

correct.rationale: At fixed volume and amount, P is proportional to the Kelvin temperature. Tripling P triples T: 3 × 300 K = 900 K, which is 900 − 273 = 627°C.

wrong.rationale: This triples the Celsius temperature, 3 × 27. Pressure is proportional to the Kelvin temperature, so the 300 K must triple to 900 K, which is 627°C.
wrong.error_pattern: multiplies the Celsius temperature instead of the Kelvin temperature

wrong.rationale: This triples the Kelvin temperature correctly to 900 K but reports it as 900°C. Converting back subtracts 273, giving 627°C.
wrong.error_pattern: forgets to convert the final kelvin value back to Celsius

wrong.rationale: This divides the Celsius temperature by 3, treating pressure as inversely related to temperature. Pressure rises with temperature at fixed volume, so T must triple to 900 K, which is 627°C.
wrong.error_pattern: inverts the relationship and uses the Celsius scale

change_note: Inverse problem: find the temperature for a given pressure ratio, with kelvin conversion in both directions; same concept as the seed.
